newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - European stocks fall as Dow tumble resumes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - European stocks fall as Dow tumble resumes.

text.p: European stock markets fell back on Wednesday as Wall Street resumed its heavy correction after a brief upturn proved to be a false dawn.

Leading European bourses staged half-hearted rallies in the morning, encouraged by a modest overnight rise on the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which had lost almost 300 points in the previous two sessions.
But predictions that only the brave would buy proved correct as European markets started falling even before Wall Street opened at mid-afternoon.

The U.S. opening only confirmed the Europeans' worst fears. The Dow tumbled another 57.41 points or 0.87 percent in the first hour to 6,553.27 and the New York Stock Exchange briefly imposed curbs on programme trades.
Among leading European markets, Germany was the worst hit. The blue-chip DAX index managed to hold on to the modest morning gains to close up 5.98 points at 3,301.91.
But that gave a false impression as German floor trade closes early. The bloodletting came in later electronic trade when the IBIS index closed down 70.52 points or 2.15 percent at 3,210.94.
London closed down a more modest 0.27 percent on the FTSE-100 index but the Paris CAC-40 shed 2.0 percent.
Recent talk that European markets would "de-couple" from Wall Street and go their own way has come to nothing.
Investors throughout the Western world are transfixed by the possibility of a further U.S. interest rate rise and what that would do to the lengthy bull run on stocks.

The question everyone tried to answer on Wednesday was whether the markets were undergoing a healthy correction after months of spectacular gains, or the early stages of something more serious and longer lasting.
Strategist David Aserkoff of Credit Suisse First Boston was more optimistic than most.

"I'd say we're at or very close to the end of the correction in the U.S. and in U.K. and European markets," said Aserkoff, who cut his mid-year target for the FTSE 100 to 4,200 from 4,425. "But just because they stop going down doesn't mean they'll start going up," he added. Chris Chaitow, technical analyst at Robert Fleming Securities, was gloomy about the FTSE, which has lost about four percent in the past four weeks from its intra-day record of 4,466. "It could now go down to 3,800," he said.
The FTSE-100 closed down 11.5 points on Wednesday at 4,236.6.
One man will play a leading role in deciding whether the plunge is a blip on an upward graph or the end to the bull run -- U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.

The U.S. central bank has already raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in a pre-emptive strike against inflation. The March rise was widely expected but now investors are beginning to speculate that the Fed might tighten policy again in May.
"In New York, the bull has developed into a huge stomping creature and Greenspan is trying to tame it," said one London dealer. "We're looking for a couple more rate increases."

The market is awaiting U.S. employment data at the end of the week for any further signs of inflationary pressures which might prompt Greenspan to try to cool the economy. "A bad payrolls number could really hurt and so everyone is wary," one dealer said.
On the foreign exchange market, the dollar was steady against the mark and reversed early weakness against the yen to close well above overnight lows of 121.35 yen.
Dealers were nervous as U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will visit Tokyo on Friday amid signs of fresh tensions over the huge Japanese trade surplus.

"There are fears in the market that the U.S. might re-think the strong dollar policy and that has depressed sentiment for dollar bulls," said Klaus Kusber, foreign exchange analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
"The market will be nervous. Japanese trade is coming back, very quickly, into market focus," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
By the European close, the dollar was at 122.70 yen, little changed from 122.60 at the European close on Tuesday. It firmed to 1.6713 marks from 1.6699.
CURRENCIES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was at 1.6713 marks and 122.70 yen compared with 1.6699 and 122.60 in late European trade on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 11.5 points, or 0.27 percent, at 4,236.6.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed down 51.54 points, or 2.0 percent, at 2,530.28.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed up 5.98 points, or 0.18 percent, at 3,301.91. In later electronic trade, the IBIS index closed down 70.52 points or 2.15 percent at 3,210.94.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $351.35 an ounce, compared with a morning fixing of $350.70 and Tuesday's close of $350.45. Silver was four cents lower at $5.00.
